pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The fungus, Fusarium sambucinum (teleomorph: Gibberella pulicaris ), survives in soil and diseased plants

type_of_disease.quote: The fungus, Fusarium sambucinum (teleomorph: Gibberella pulicaris )

affected_parts.quote: Canker disease leads to yellowing of leaves and generally unthrifty growth. Affected bines wilt rapidly and suddenly... Cankers can be found on rhizomes of affected plants.

summary.value: Yellowing of leaves and unthrifty growth, with affected bines wilting rapidly and suddenly (often at flowering or in hot weather); the bine base is typically swollen and may have a longitudinal split, and bines detach easily from the crown.
summary.quote: Canker disease leads to yellowing of leaves and generally unthrifty growth. Affected bines wilt rapidly and suddenly; often at flowering or during hot weather. Bines can detach and readily break from the crown with a gentle tug.

diagnostic_features.value: Swollen bine base with a narrow, tapered/rounded point of attachment to the crown (only a few central vascular elements connect bine to crown), bines that break off with a gentle tug, sometimes a longitudinal split in the cortical area, and an absence of vascular discoloration.
diagnostic_features.quote: The point of bine attachment to the crown usually is tapered or rounded off so that only a few central vascular elements connect the bine to the crown... The bine's base is typically swollen because carbohydrate movement has been inhibited; sometimes affected stems have a longitudinal split in the colonized cortical area of the bine. Vascular discoloration does not seem to be associated with the disease.

value: Verticillium wilt
look_alikes.quote: Wilted bines could potentially be confused with wilt caused by Verticillium species. The pattern of necrosis on leaves and vascular discoloration associated with Verticillium infection differentiates Verticillium wilt from canker.

value: Avoid injury to hop plants.
Chemical pruning in the spring reduced canker disease severity compared to mechanical pruning, but no difference was detected in Oregon field studies.
Hilling up the plants enhances adventitious root growth above cankered bine portions, which can help maintain bine vigor and cone yield.
Reduce crown wetness by hilling higher relative to rill irrigation ditches, by removing sucker growth that could shade the crown, and by reducing mulch.
Lime to increase soil pH above 7.
Maintain the higher pH by using less ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizer; use nitrate-based fertilizer instead.
Mefenoxam applications are not an effective chemical treatment for Fusarium canker based on studies by OSU.
Asperello at 1.5 to 10.7 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals as a foliar spray or at 0.1 to 0.7 oz/100 gal water on 8- to 12-week intervals for chemigation at 2,000 to 5,000 gal/A.
Bio-Tam 2 at 2.5 to 3 lb/A as a banded ground spray or at 2.5 to 5 lb/A on 14- to 21-day intervals for chemigation.
Bexfond at 7 to 14 fl oz/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation, reapply on 4-week intervals.
Theia at 1 to 5 lb/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation.
treatments.quote: Avoid injury to hop plants. Studies by OSU and the USDA-ARS in the state of Washington showed that chemical pruning in the spring reduced canker disease severity compared to mechanical pruning... Lime to increase soil pH above 7. Maintain the higher pH by using less ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizer; use nitrate-based fertilizer instead.

value: Exclusion is an important means of virus control.
Use virus-tested stock certified to be free of viruses.
Clean rootstock is available from the Clean Plant Center Northwest at https://cpcnw.wsu.edu/
Plant where hops have not been grown before or in fields where all hop plants have died out.
General sanitation for disease control.
Work/harvest diseased yards last.
Clean equipment between yards, particularly during early season operations.
Currently, it is recommended that equipment be cleaned by first washing to remove plant debris and then with a 5% to 10% bleach solution for at least a few seconds to upwards of 10 minutes.
Destroy plants that are severely stunted or yellowed.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Powdery mildew is caused by a fungus, Podosphaera macularis (formerly Sphaerotheca humuli )

type_of_disease.quote: Powdery mildew is caused by a fungus, Podosphaera macularis

value: Foliar
Stem
Whole plant
affected_parts.quote: new shoots can be covered with the powdery mildew fungus, and the entire shoot may appear white. These "flagshoots" produce conidia... Secondary infections on susceptible leaves appear as whitish, powdery spots on either the upper or lower leaf surface... Flowers and cones of susceptible varieties may be infected.

summary.value: New shoots can be entirely covered with the fungus and appear white ("flagshoots"); secondary infections on leaves appear as whitish, powdery spots on upper or lower leaf surfaces, sometimes preceded by a small blister. Infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, and infected areas on cones become red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
summary.quote: new shoots can be covered with the powdery mildew fungus, and the entire shoot may appear white. These "flagshoots" produce conidia, which initiate secondary infections. Secondary infections on susceptible leaves appear as whitish, powdery spots on either the upper or lower leaf surface. Entire leaf surfaces can be covered with powdery mildew. Depending on the hop variety and leaf age, initially a small blister may form before the fungus is visible.

diagnostic_features.value: White, circular powdery colonies on leaves; entire white shoots (flagshoots) typical in spring; infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, leading to cone shatter, with infected areas becoming red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
diagnostic_features.quote: Note the white, circular colonies... Flag shoots, such as the one above, are typical in the spring... Infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, leading to cone shatter and uneven crop maturity... Infected areas on cones become red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.

value: Reduce or eliminate infected buds and flag shoots by crowning, harrowing, burning, etc. Treating before shoots emerge reduces early-season spread within a field.
Completely removing green tissue during preparation for training reduces spore load and subsequent secondary spread.
Maintain adequate nitrogen levels but do not over-apply because more succulent tissue is more susceptible.
Scout yards regularly for signs of powdery mildew.
Control bottom growth after training, mechanically or with burn-back herbicides, etc., in order to reduce active colonies.
Strip lower leaves up to about 4 ft in order to break the "green bridge" that facilitates powdery mildew's climb up in the canopy.
Early harvest can reduce powdery mildew losses in fields with high disease pressure.
Remove seedlings from around harvesting shed and hop dryer. Remove pole plants. Eliminate feral hops.
Protect regrowth against infection or remove shoot regrowth (mow, desiccate, flail, flame, etc.).
Replace highly susceptible varieties.
Thorough spray coverage is essential to protect hop plants; spray every row. Apply protective fungicides before disease is reproducing and spreading.
Bicarbonates are registered to control powdery mildew (Bi-Carb Old Fashioned Fungicide, HO Carb-O-Nator, Kaligreen, MilStop SP, Vacres).

Demethylation-inhibiting (DMI) Fungicides (Group 3) are labeled for use. Alternate or tank-mix with a non-Group 3 fungicide for resistance management (Procure 480SC, Rally 40WSP, Rhyme, Sonoma 40WSP, Tebustar 3.6L, Tebuzol 3.6F, Topguard).
Luna Experience (Group 7 + 3), Luna Sensation (Group 7 + 11), Magister SC (Group 39).
Oils are labeled to control hop powdery mildew (IAP Organic 440 Spray Oil, JMS Stylet Oil, 440 Superior Spray Oil, Trilogy).
Quintec (Group 13).
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5).
Strobilurin fungicides (Group 11) are labeled for use (Flint Extra, Pristine).
Sulfur formulations are registered for hop (Microthiol Disperss, Proganic Micronized Sulfur); primarily a protectant and must be applied before infection.
Torino (Group U6).
Biological control (Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Ecoswing, Romeo, Sonata) â€” efficacy unknown in the Pacific Northwest.
treatments.quote: Cultural control These management strategies aim to reduce overwintering and buildup of early-season disease inoculum... Chemical control Thorough spray coverage is essential to protect hop plants; spray every row. Apply protective fungicides before disease is reproducing and spreading.
